name: Erik Gupta

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for seeing me, Erik. I'm with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We have no ties to AI companies, employers, unions or government, and what you say stays confidential. Can you describe a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I run the pig side at Brennan Farm. That's 200 outdoor sows in huts on the lower fields, plus we grow potatoes and barley on the rest. I'm out by six doing feed and water, checking farrowing huts, which is where the sows have their litters, then moving electric fence or loading pigs for market. In autumn I'm on the potato harvester till dark.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What do you like about it, and what wears you out?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I like that I'm good at it. The Brennans know if I say a sow's off, she's off. What wears me out is the pig price, because it goes up and down like a yo-yo and when it's down, everyone's tight, me included. I live on my own in a flat above the shop in Marlow Bridge, I've got a car loan, and I've got maybe a month of money if I'm careful.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That sounds about right to me. Most new stuff turns out to be less than they said.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I wouldn't say much, to be honest. Maybe 'there you go' to Ray, the tractor driver, at break. I don't post things online, I'd rather say it to someone's face.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It means nothing changes for me, and nothing changing still isn't great. When the pig price dropped last year, the Brennans let one lad go and I picked up his work for the same pay. That can happen again with or without AI.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd carry on as I am. I'd try to put an extra eighty a month on the car loan so it's gone by next summer. That's about it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Fine, mostly. A bit on edge, like always. It's the pig price that bothers me, not robots.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: When the Brennans let that lad go, how did you feel about it?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Not happy, but I understood. When the pig price is that low, Brennan Farm loses money on every pig that goes out the gate. If I owned the place I'd probably have done the same.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would happen if the pig price dropped again next year?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Probably more hours for the same money, again. I wouldn't lose my job, I don't think, because they need someone who knows the sows. But I'd lose my evenings.

say: I'd just say **'there you go'** to Ray at break.
I **don't post** anything online, because I'd rather say it to someone's face.
think: Nothing changing still isn't great, because the **pig price** swings.
Last year a lad was let go and I took on his work for the **same pay**.
do: Carry on with the **pig unit** as normal.
Pay an extra **eighty a month** on the car loan to clear it by summer.
feel: Fine, but a bit **on edge** about the pig price.
S0.quote: When the pig price is that low, Brennan Farm loses money on every pig that goes out the gate.
fieldNote: He's **matter-of-fact** and doesn't blame the owners for cutting staff.
The **pig price cycle**, not AI, is his real background pressure.
He expects to keep his job but lose **evenings and hours** in a bad year.

steps.text: Keep running the 200 outdoor sows as now
Overpay the car loan by eighty a month to clear it by summer

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That sounds more like real life. Things change, but not overnight.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd probably say the office side will change but someone still has to walk the fields. Not much more than that. I'd leave the big talk to others.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, it barely touches me for a few years. The Brennans' daughter Ciara does the paperwork, and she'd use AI for ordering and pig passports, which are the movement records. My bit is boots and buckets.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep doing what I do. I'd keep paying off the car. If Ciara wanted me to use some app for the sows, I'd ask her to put it in for me and I'd just tell her the numbers.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Not worried, really. A bit wary, like when a new owner takes over the shop downstairs.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You don't use AI tools at all. Would that ever become a problem for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Maybe one day. But I've seen apps come and go on this farm, and the pigs still need feeding at six. I'd rather wait and see which ones last.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who on the farm would you worry about?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ciara, if anything, because her job is the one the computer can do. She's clever, though; she'd find something. Ray's sixty, so he'll retire before any robot drives that tractor.

say: I'd say the office will change but **someone still walks** the fields.
I'd **leave the big talk** to others.
think: It barely touches me for **a few years**.
AI would take Ciara's **paperwork**, while my work is **boots and buckets**.
do: Keep running the pig unit **as normal**.
Ask Ciara to **enter the data** for any new app while he gives her numbers.
Wait to see which tools **actually last**.
S1.quote: I've seen apps come and go on this farm, and the pigs still need feeding at six.
fieldNote: He correctly sees his job as **mostly hands-on** and slow to change.
He thinks the **office worker**, Ciara, is most exposed.
His strategy is to **wait and see** which tools survive.

steps.text: Keep up feeding, farrowing checks and market loading as normal
Leave new pig apps to Ciara until one proves itself

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Two years. Then robots in five. That's fast.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say someone needs to think about people like me, because it's coming whether we like it or not. I'd say it to Ray and to my dad. Still wouldn't post anything.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If I'm honest, I think I'm out of a job by 2031 or soon after. If a robot can check farrowing huts and load pigs as well as me and never asks for a day off, the Brennans would be stupid not to buy one. I've got a month of money and a car loan, so that keeps me up.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: First I'd cut back hard: no takeaways, cheaper phone, and clear the car loan however I can. Then I'd ask my mum and dad if I could move back into my old room near Ashton if it came to it. After AGI arrives, I'd start looking at the council's road crew, because I don't see robots fixing potholes for a while.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Sick to my stomach, a bit. I'm not one for big feelings, but that one gets me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would the three years between the AI and the robots mean for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Three more years of wages, I suppose. That's three years to pay the car off and save something. I wouldn't spend them learning about computers, though, I'd spend them earning.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to your parents?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell my dad straight that I might need my old room back. My dad drove lorries for thirty years and he'd say robots are just another boss. My mum would just put the kettle on.

say: I'd say someone needs to think about **people like me**.
I'd talk to Ray and my dad, but **not post** anything.
think: I expect to be **out of a job** by 2031 or soon after.
The Brennans would be **stupid not to buy** a robot that never takes a day off.
do: **Cut spending** on takeaways and his phone, and clear the car loan.
Ask his parents about **moving back** into his old room.
Look at the council's **road crew** after AGI arrives.
feel: **Sick** to his stomach, which is unusual for him.
S2.quote: If a robot can check farrowing huts and load pigs as well as me and never asks for a day off, the Brennans would be stupid not to buy one.
fieldNote: He **doesn't blame** the owners, even when he expects to be replaced.
He'd use the **three-year gap** to earn and save, not to retrain.
Family is his **safety net**: his old room at his parents'.

steps.text: Cancel takeaways, switch to a cheaper phone plan, clear the car loan
Ask his parents if he can move back into his old room
Apply to the council road crew once AGI arrives

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years, then robots in about eight. Still quick, but you'd see it coming.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say the same as before, that somebody has to plan for people who work with their hands. Probably say it at the pub, not online.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Really, I think it's the same ending, just a bit later. I'd have the car paid off and maybe a few months saved by then. I'd be thirty-five and wondering what I'm good for besides pigs.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd save hard for the first few years, maybe a hundred a month. I'd keep an eye out, and around 2032 I'd start looking at other work, like the road crew or the grain store in Ashton. Until then I'd keep my head down.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Worried, but it's a slow worry. Like a sow you know will lose condition over winter.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd wait until 2032. Why not start looking now?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because there's nothing better around here now. Brennan Farm pays badly but it's the best pig job in thirty miles. Leaving early would just make things worse sooner.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you want to be doing at thirty-five?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Still pigs, if I'm honest. But if not pigs, then something outside, with my hands. I'd go mad in an office, and I don't think the office will be there anyway.

say: I'd say somebody has to plan for **people who work** with their hands.
I'd say it at the **pub**, not online.
think: It's the **same ending**, just a bit later.
At thirty-five I'd wonder what I'm **good for besides pigs**.
do: Save **a hundred a month** for the first few years.
Start looking at the **road crew** or the Ashton grain store around 2032.
Keep his **head down** at Brennan Farm until then.
S3.quote: Brennan Farm pays badly but it's the best pig job in thirty miles.
fieldNote: More warning helps him **save**, but doesn't change his plan much.
**Few local jobs** make leaving early feel pointless.
He wants to stay **outdoors and hands-on** whatever happens.

steps.text: Save a hundred a month once the car loan is paid
Stay at Brennan Farm until around 2032 before looking elsewhere
Apply to the Ashton grain store or council road crew around 2032

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years? I'd be thirty-seven. That's a long way off.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is plenty of time for people to sort it out. I'd probably say I'll worry about it in 2035.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I think it means I've got a decade of pigs left, and that's not bad. By 2039 I'd want a bit saved and a plan B. But I'm not going to tear up my life now for something ten years out.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd carry on, pay off the car, and start saving once it's paid. Around 2035 I'd think about what's next. Maybe a short course in something outdoors, like hedge laying, but only if I had to.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Fine, mostly. It's far enough off that I don't think about it every day.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You've said you'd decide around 2035. What would make you decide sooner?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If the Brennans bought a robot for anything, I'd sit up. Or if Ciara started talking about it. Until a robot shows up on Brennan Farm, it's just news to me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there anything you'd change now, even with ten years?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Maybe I'd stop putting off getting my HGV licence, which lets you drive big lorries. My dad's been on at me about it for years. It's good to have something else in your back pocket.

say: I'd say **ten years** is plenty of time to sort it out.
I'd say I'll **worry about it** in 2035.
think: I've got **a decade of pigs** left, and that's not bad.
I'm not going to **tear up my life** for something ten years out.
do: Keep working the pig unit and **clear the car** loan.
Consider getting his **HGV licence** as a back-up.
feel: **Fine**, mostly, because it's far enough off not to think about daily.
S4.quote: Until a robot shows up on Brennan Farm, it's just news to me.
fieldNote: With ten years he is **close to relaxed** and resists planning.
A **robot on the farm** would be his trigger to act.
The **HGV licence** is a plan B his dad has pushed for years.

steps.text: Keep running the pigs and finish paying off the car
Wait until about 2035, or a robot on the farm, before planning
Get an HGV lorry licence as a back-up

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028, because there's no time and no money. What would help is honest notice from the Brennans if they're buying robots, and some help with the cost of a new licence or course. Not handouts, just a fair start at something else.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Not really. Maybe ask about the pigs. A good pigman knows when a sow is going to lie on the piglets before it happens. I'd like to see a robot learn that.

headlineQuote: A good pigman knows when a sow is going to lie on the piglets before it happens.
portrait: Erik, 27, runs the **outdoor pig unit** on a mixed farm, living alone above the village shop.
He has about **a month** of savings and a car loan, and the pig price swings already squeeze him.
He's practical, **doesn't blame** owners, and never uses AI tools.
He'd lean on his **parents** and look for outdoor council work if robots came fast.
His mood runs from uneasy to **alarmed** under fast AGI, and back to uneasy with ten years.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, with no time and no money to adjust.
whatWouldHelp: **Honest notice** from the Brennans before they buy robots.
Help with the cost of a **new licence** or course, not handouts.
